skill.name: autopilot
skill.description: Builds applications and features through structured briefing, specification, planning, delegated implementation, review, acceptance, and project memory.
skill.summary: Turns a product brief into a reviewed, tested project with tracked requirements and progress.
skill.author: nick-vels

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives from Markdown formatting, JavaScript template literals, secret-redaction guidance, CSS, and embedded PNG logos. One command risk is confirmed: shutdown trusts a PID from a writable file, and the loopback dashboard server briefly exposes all run artifacts to the local host.

remediation.issue: Server shutdown trusts an unverified PID from .autopilot/serve.pid.
remediation.suggestion: Before signaling the PID, verify its start time, command, working directory, and bound port. Store a random run token and refuse cleanup when identity checks fail.

remediation.issue: The temporary server exposes the full .autopilot directory on loopback.
remediation.suggestion: Serve a dedicated directory containing only dashboard.html and a minimized state file. Exclude briefs, specifications, manifests, and tickets from the document root.

semantic_findings.title: Loopback Server Exposes Run Artifacts Locally
semantic_findings.description: The preview path serves the entire .autopilot directory, including briefs, manifests, specifications, and tickets. Other same-host users or processes can read these artifacts while the server runs.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The instructions explicitly serve .autopilot and acknowledge that it contains run artifacts. Loopback binding prevents remote access but does not isolate data from the local host.

medium_findings.title: Shell command substitution
medium_findings.confidence_reasoning: The shutdown command trusts a PID read from a writable project file and sends it a signal without verifying the process identity. A stale or modified serve.pid could terminate an unrelated local process.

content.user_title: Build Complete Software Projects on Autopilot
content.value_statement: Complex builds often lose requirements between the brief, implementation, and review. Autopilot tracks each requirement through a structured, delegated delivery workflow.
actual_capabilities: Converts a dictated brief into a numbered manifest, specification, interfaces, and implementation tickets.
Supports full, semi, interview, and manual workflows with strict, normal, or deep elaboration.
Delegates implementation tickets to subagents and requires testing, review, repair, and separate commits.
Creates a local dashboard that tracks stages, tickets, timings, tests, assumptions, and placeholders.
Runs independent coverage and acceptance checks, then records project memory and architectural decisions.
limitations: Designed for repository-based projects, not small single-file edits or line-by-line collaboration.
Requires filesystem, Git, command, browser, and subagent access for the complete workflow.
Autonomous modes can modify many files and create local commits without intermediate approval.
Deployment, publishing, payment, messaging, deletion, and history rewriting always require confirmation.

use_cases.title: Create a Founder Prototype
use_cases.description: Turn a clear product idea into a tested local project without requiring the founder to review technical artifacts.

use_cases.title: Deliver a Repository Feature
use_cases.description: Map an existing feature brief to requirements, interfaces, implementation tickets, tests, and review.

use_cases.title: Control an Autonomous Build
use_cases.description: Use manual gates for specification and planning while keeping implementation, review, and acceptance delegated.

prompt_templates.title: Build a Simple Project
prompt_templates.prompt: Use Autopilot to build [project] for [audience]. It must support [core requirements]. Use the default workflow and keep the result local.
prompt_templates.scenario: A beginner has a clear idea and wants a complete local project.

prompt_templates.title: Add a Feature
prompt_templates.prompt: Use Autopilot in semi mode to add [feature] to this repository. Preserve the existing stack and satisfy [acceptance criteria].
prompt_templates.scenario: An existing project needs a scoped feature with limited questions.

prompt_templates.title: Develop the Brief Deeply
prompt_templates.prompt: Use Autopilot in interview and deep modes for [product]. Challenge unclear assumptions, ask every important product question, then complete the build.
prompt_templates.scenario: The product direction needs structured discovery before implementation.

prompt_templates.title: Run a Controlled High-Fidelity Build
prompt_templates.prompt: Use Autopilot in manual, strict, and polish modes. Build only [requirements], obtain approval for the specification and tickets, then compare against [reference].
prompt_templates.scenario: An advanced user wants explicit gates, strict scope, and reference-based refinement.

output_examples.input: Build a local appointment application for a small studio with services, available times, and contact details.
output: A reviewed local application covering booking, availability, validation, and empty states.
A requirement manifest showing what was completed, deferred, or left as a placeholder.
A final report with test results, assumptions, setup steps, and remaining configuration.

output_examples.input: Add CSV customer import to the existing product. Reject invalid rows and report partial failures.
output: A feature integrated with the existing stack and repository conventions.
Tests covering valid imports, invalid rows, duplicates, and partial failures.
Independent acceptance results traced back to the original brief.

output_examples.input: Interview me about a delivery marketplace, then build the approved scope.
output_examples.output: A structured interview resolves product forks before the skill writes the specification, delegates implementation, reviews each ticket, and reports acceptance.

best_practices: State the audience, core workflow, constraints, and success conditions in the initial brief.
Use manual mode when specification or ticket approval is important to project governance.
Review placeholders, assumptions, environment variable names, and deferred requirements in the final report.
anti_patterns: Do not use Autopilot for a tiny single-file change that needs no specification or delegation.
Do not place secret values in the brief, repository, prompts, dashboard state, or final report.
Do not request deployment or other outward actions without an explicit confirmation step.

faq.question: Does Autopilot ask questions?
faq.answer: Semi mode asks only about genuine product forks. Full mode self-briefs, while interview and manual modes ask more questions.

faq.question: Can I approve the specification before coding starts?
faq.answer: Yes. Manual mode waits for explicit approval of both the specification and the implementation tickets.

faq.question: Will it deploy or publish the result automatically?
faq.answer: No. Deployment, publishing, payment, external messaging, deletion, and history rewriting require explicit confirmation in every mode.

faq.question: How does it track progress?
faq.answer: It writes local run state and displays stages, tickets, tests, timings, assumptions, and placeholders in a dashboard.

faq.question: How are secrets handled?
faq.answer: The workflow records variable names only, redacts pasted values, and instructs the user to configure secrets in an ignored environment file.

faq.question: What remains after the build?
faq.answer: The repository contains run records, project memory, local commits, test results, and architectural decisions when the project tier requires them.
